title: Why Are We So Obsessed With Whether Someone Used AI to Write, Who Cares
author: Ludwig, Bette
summary: Prompted by her own experience of being falsely accused of using AI to write a Substack post (an AI-detector flagged it as '100% AI-generated' when it wasn't), the author surveys the chaos of AI-detection policy across education and publishing. Her central point is that no institution agrees on the rules: University of Chicago is banning devices, UT Austin is encouraging AI use, UC Berkeley bans it entirely including brainstorming, and New York just banned generative AI outright in grades K-8 after previously being pro-technology. She extends the same incoherence to publishing, where outlets like The Chronicle ban AI use entirely while others like Pharmacy Times allow it with disclosure, and many have no policy at all. The piece's real argument is that 'AI slop' has become a social accusation rather than a measurable category — readers, editors, and detection tools all claim authority to judge it, and none of them agree, with the detection tool in her own case being definitively wrong. She closes by admitting that even as an AI advocate, the incoherence and hostility of the current moment is making her sympathetic to the same 'pause' argument being made by Anthropic's CEO.
points: Documents wildly inconsistent AI policy across higher ed in the same year: UChicago bans devices, UT Austin embraces AI, UC Berkeley bans even AI-assisted brainstorming.
Notes New York's K-8 generative-AI ban as the strictest K-12 policy she's tracked, a full reversal from the state's earlier pro-tech stance.
Uses her own false-positive AI-detection flag (Pangram wrongly scored her human-written post as 100% AI) as proof that detection tools cannot be trusted as arbiters.
Argues that 'AI slop' functions as a social accusation rather than a verifiable judgment — readers, editors, and detectors all claim the authority to call it, and none of them agree.
quotes: Pangram flagged my post as 100% AI-generated, even though it was not. But that didn't matter to the readers who felt compelled to comment.

The University of Chicago banning electronics, so they aren't allowing phones or laptops anymore in their first-year classes. The University of Texas is outwardly encouraging using AI with their faculty and staff. UC Berkeley is banning it completely, including brainstorming.

K-12 is going through its own identity crisis with this technology. The most recent comes from New York banning generative AI in K-8, which is the highest that I have seen so far. They have done a complete 180.

So how and who gets to decide what's boring AI slop? Readers, apparently, even when they can't name a single sentence that tipped them off. Editors at outlets that still don't have a written policy. Or Pangram, a detection tool that flagged my original post as 100% AI-generated and was flat wrong.

This past weekend, the CEO of Anthropic came out urging the world to pump the brakes on AI. I'm a strong advocate for AI, but even I am starting to feel like we need to start hitting the pause button, folks.
